title: Given the roots of two binary trees, determine whether they are structurally identical and have the same values at every corresponding node.
shortTitle: Same Tree: check if two trees are identical
keyPoints: Two trees are the same if both nodes are null, or both are non-null with equal values and identical subtrees
The both-null check must come before the one-null check to avoid false negatives
Logical AND short-circuits so a mismatch anywhere stops the comparison early
Time is O(min(n1, n2)) because a structural mismatch halts the recursion; space is O(h)
For object-valued nodes, use .equals() instead of == to compare values correctly
The same pattern applies to verifying that two independently maintained hierarchies match exactly

s1_definition.oneliner: Two trees are the same if both nodes are null, or both are non-null with equal values and identical left and right subtrees.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Same Tree** checks whether two binary trees are identical in both shape and node values.
- **Parallel recursion** walks both trees in lockstep, visiting corresponding positions together.
- **Both-null** at a position means it matches; **one-null** means the structures diverge.
- **Short-circuit AND** collapses the result to false on the first mismatch in shape or value.
- **Time** is O(min(n1, n2)) because a mismatch halts early; **space** is O(h) for the call stack.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has two copies of the National Bank of India's branch org chart, one from head office and one from the local branch, and he needs to verify they match exactly before an audit. He walks both charts in lockstep. At each position, either both charts have no one there, or both have the same person. If one chart has a manager where the other is empty, or the names differ, the charts are not the same and the audit fails immediately.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Parallel recursion on two trees
  ================================

  Tree A:     1        Tree B:     1
             / \                  / \
            2    3               2    3

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Compare(1, 1)                      │
  │  ├── both non-null, vals equal      │
  │  ├── Compare(2, 2)                  │
  │  │   ├── both non-null, vals equal  │
  │  │   ├── Compare(null, null) → true │
  │  │   └── Compare(null, null) → true │
  │  └── Compare(3, 3)                  │
  │      ├── both non-null, vals equal  │
  │      ├── Compare(null, null) → true │
  │      └── Compare(null, null) → true │
  │  Result: true                       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  Decision at each position:
  ┌────────────────────────────────┐
  │ both null?       → true        │
  │ one null?        → false       │
  │ values differ?   → false       │
  │ else → recurse left AND right  │
  └────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Same Tree is a parallel recursion problem where you walk two trees in lockstep and verify that every corresponding position matches in both structure and value. The recursion has two base cases whose order matters: first, if both nodes are null, this position matches and you return true; second, if exactly one is null, the structures diverge and you return false. Only after passing both do you compare the values at the current position.

If the values match, you recurse into both left subtrees and both right subtrees, combining the results with a logical AND that short-circuits. The moment any position mismatches in shape or value, the comparison stops and the whole result collapses to false. This fail-fast behavior is exactly what you want when most comparisons either match fully or differ early.

The time complexity is O(min(n1, n2)) because a structural mismatch halts the recursion early, and a full match visits every node once. The space is O(h) from the call stack. For object-valued nodes, always use the `.equals()` method rather than reference equality.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in a hierarchy audit service. Two independent systems maintain the branch approval hierarchy, and before an audit the two trees are verified to be identical. A silent divergence could mean an unauthorized approver was inserted, so the lockstep comparison fails fast on the first difference and raises a severe alert pointing the compliance team straight at the problem.

Remember one sentence: walk two trees in lockstep, check both-null before one-null, compare values, and short-circuit AND the subtree results.
